extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature and history; creative writers interested in heroic figures and moral/historical argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and codifies Carlyle's evaluative principles about heroes, hero-worship, reformers, and sincerity that inform how heroic figures and their historical roles should be represented or judged in narrative and essay. Useful for writers and critics modelling heroic characterization and moral-historical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Poet and Reformer (modes of heroism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mild shining of the Poet's light has to give place to the fierce lightning of the Reformer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poet and reformer as distinct heroic functions: the Poet tempers and teaches by music and mildness; the Reformer acts fiercely when necessary. Use poetic/musical methods where possible, but recognize the need for violent, decisive action when institutions become obstructive. Example: Reformers are 'needful and inevitable' when former advancements ossify into obstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finished Poet as symptom of an epoch's completion
rubrics_metrics.description: The finished Poet ... is a symptom that his epoch itself has reached perfection and is finished; that before long there will be a new epoch, new Reformers needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In representing cultural moments, portray the 'perfect' poet not only as culmination but as herald of impending change; a consummate poetic art signals historical completion and opens space for reformist energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer musical/equable reform but accept necessity of violent reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Could we go along always in the way of music... or failing this rhythmic musical way, how good were it could we get so much as into the equable way; ... But it is not so... the battling Reformer too is, from time to time, a needful and inevitable phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for gradual, peaceful reform in depictions when possible; nevertheless dramatize and justify confrontational reform as an inevitable remedy when subtler methods fail and obstructions have accumulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief as prerequisite for faithful action
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who will do faithfully, needs to believe firmly. If he have to ask at every turn the world's suffrage... the work committed to him will be mis-done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize effective agents (heroes, reformers, workers) as firmly believing in their cause; doubt and dependence on public approval lead to compromised, dishonest, or ineffective action. Show consequences of half-belief: moral paralysis, accumulation of offences, eventual revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of offences leads to explosive revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Offences accumulate till they become insupportable; and are then violently burst through, cleared off as by explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting social change, show a build-up of small corruptions and compromises that inexorably produce a dramatic rupture. Use historical examples (e.g., Dante → Luther; Feudalism → French Revolution) to justify sudden upheaval as response to long-term moral/structural decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction as new creation; endurance of essential truth
rubrics_metrics.description: All destruction, by violent revolution or howsoever it be, is but new creation on a wider scale. No thought that ever dwelt honestly as true in the heart of man but was an honest insight into God's truth ... and has an essential truth in it which endures through all changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating earlier beliefs as wholly worthless; portray continuity of essential truths beneath changing forms. In narrative, demolition of old forms should be depicted as preparatory to a truer and larger order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject chauvinistic teleologies that declare all past generations wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: What a melancholy notion is that, which has to represent all men ... as having spent their life in blind condemnable error ... It is an incredible hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write heroes or histories that assert present generation's absolute superiority by consigning past peoples to simple error. Show complexity and partial truth in prior systems to give reforms moral legitimacy and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity among sincere men across different uniforms/traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are not all true men that live, or that ever lived, soldiers of the same army ... Why should we misknow one another, fight not against the enemy but against ourselves, from mere difference of uniform? All uniforms shall be good, so they hold in them true valiant men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating inter-tradition alliances or comparing heroes, foreground sincerity and valor as the basis of fellowship rather than institutional trappings. Emphasize shared moral aims over surface differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idolatry defined and condemned when insincere (Cant / Sincere‑Cant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Idol is Eidolon ... All worship whatsoever must proceed by Symbols, ... Where, then, lies the evil of it? ... Condemnable Idolatry is insincere Idolatry. Doubt has eaten out the heart of it: ... 'You only believe that you believe.' ... It is equivalent to ... Formulism, and Worship of Formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between sincere symbolic practice (which can be meritorious) and insincere/formulaic worship (which is morally corrosive). In characterization, show the ruinous effects of 'sincere-cant' — people pretending belief — as the root of immorality and social decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero as breaker of idols; return to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the property of every Hero ... that he come back to reality; that he stand upon things, and not shows of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray heroes as truth‑tellers who expose and demolish hollow institutions and ceremonial falseness. Use concrete symbolic acts (e.g., burning a papal bull) to dramatize the hero's return to 'realities' over 'shows'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private judgment (individual conscience) does not imply anarchy if sincere
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercise of private judgment, faithfully gone about, does by no means necessarily end in selfish independence, isolation; but rather ends necessarily in the opposite of that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting the rise of private judgment, show how genuine, sincere conviction fosters unity and true communion, whereas insincerity and half-belief produce fragmentation and anarchy. Emphasize moral interiority as a source of social cohesion in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit of originality is sincerity, not mere novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of originality is not novelty; it is sincerity. The believing man is the original man; whatsoever he believes, he believes it for himself, not for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value characters' heartfelt conviction over mere innovation. In narrative, reward authenticity of belief and action rather than flashy newness unbacked by sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero‑worship rooted in genuine reality and sincerity (not semblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero-worship never dies, nor can die. Loyalty and Sovereignty are everlasting in the world:--and there is this in them, that they are grounded not on garnitures and semblances, but on realities and sincerities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting cults of personality or reverence scenes, make clear that legitimate hero‑worship arises from real virtue and demonstrable deeds rather than from theatrical ornament or empty titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical markers of a true Hero: humble origin and acquaintance with realities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is altogether suitable to Luther's function ... that he was born poor, and brought up poor ... Hardship, rigorous Necessity was the poor boy's companion; ... Among things, not among the shows of things, had he to grow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In heroic biographies, use humble origins, material hardship, and early exposure to 'realities' (not pomp) as formative elements that legitimize later moral authority. Show how such background disciplines the hero for confronting hollow power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion/deliverance as key heroic epoch
rubrics_metrics.description: This, then, is his deliverance from darkness, his final triumph over darkness, what we call his conversion; for himself the most important of all epochs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict a clear turning point (spiritual/intellectual conversion) that reorients the hero from despair or falsehood to a settled, active mission; make the conversion credible via texts, mentors, or revelatory experiences (e.g., discovery of a Bible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courageous public defiance as criterion of heroic standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Diet of Worms ... the point, indeed, from which the whole subsequent history of civilization takes its rise ... 'Here stand I; I can do no other: God assist me!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write moments of public, principled defiance (speeches, refusals to recant) as climactic tests of heroic integrity. Show the stakes — institutional power arrayed against the individual — and the hero's resolute conscience as decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation by corrupt authority as legitimate cause of revolt
rubrics_metrics.description: The elegant Pagan Pope ... dooms the Monk's writings to be burnt ... By this fire-decree of his, had kindled into noble just wrath the bravest heart then living in this world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray corrupt or performative authorities whose actions legitimately provoke moral opposition; use such provocations to justify the hero's transition from private conscience to public action.
